meta.tagline: From golden temples to night stalls, the city that never stops

overview.title: Welcome to Bangkok
overview.intro: Bangkok is like two cities living at once: golden stupas gleam in the morning sun while the BTS train glides between skyscrapers; freight barges crawl the Chao Phraya while a street wok bursts into flame. In this city the best meals are eaten on plastic stools, the best views are drunk in from rooftop bars, and the best moments happen in unplanned corners. The heat is humid, the traffic is legendary, and a smile opens every door — calling Thailand 'the land of smiles' is not marketing, it's observation.

local_word.definition: More than the Thai word for 'fun': the philosophy of folding joy into everything. Work, food, even waiting in traffic should be done with sanuk — otherwise why do it? If a Bangkok vendor is joking behind her stall, she's not merely enjoying her job; she's living sanuk. When your plan collapses, smile: that's the most Bangkok reaction there is.

rules.title: Visit temples early and covered
rules.description: The Grand Palace and Wat Pho are cool and calm at opening; midday heat and tour crowds make both a struggle. Shoulders and knees must be covered — keep a thin scarf in your bag. Never pose with your back to a Buddha image; respect is taken seriously in this city.

rules.title: Don't fear the street stall — trust the queue
rules.description: Bangkok's kitchen is on the street: a stall with a local queue and ingredients turning before your eyes beats the safest restaurant. Wok fire is faster than any germ — anything cooked hot is your friend. Let day one start with pad thai and the last day end with something you can't name.

rules.title: Beat the traffic with rails and the river
rules.description: One hour in Bangkok traffic is eight minutes on the BTS: plan near the train and metro lines. For riverside targets, the Chao Phraya express boat is both transport and sightseeing. Ride a tuk-tuk once for the experience — not for transportation.

quick_facts.label: Currency
quick_facts.sub: Stalls take cash, malls take cards

tip.label: The Bangkok philosophy
tip.text: Here the schedule follows the heat, not the clock: temples in the morning, air-conditioned break at noon, river in the late afternoon, stalls at night. One big goal a day is enough — the spaces in between fill themselves. Jai yen yen: 'keep a cool heart', and the rest is sanuk.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Traffic is Bangkok's only enemy; the antidotes run in the sky (BTS), underground (MRT) and on the river (express boats).

items.title: Arriving from the airport
items.description: From Suvarnabhumi, the Airport Rail Link reaches the center in half an hour: cheap and traffic-free. Landing at Don Mueang means a bus or Grab. For late-night arrivals, Grab is the painless choice — at the taxi rank, use the official queue.

items.title: BTS SkyTrain and MRT
items.description: The BTS SkyTrain and the MRT metro are the city's spine: air-conditioned, punctual, immune to traffic. A Rabbit card or single-journey token — the fastest option even at rush hour. Siam station is the heart where lines meet.

items.title: The Chao Phraya express boat
items.description: Orange-flag express boats hop pier to pier along the river: the Grand Palace, Wat Arun and Chinatown all sit on the bank. A river cruise at commuter prices — skip the seat and stand at the rail.

items.title: Grab and Bolt
items.description: App rides are haggle-free and air-conditioned; for short hops, the moto-taxi option slices straight through traffic (ask for a helmet). If you take a taxi, say 'meter, please' — smile and step out if they refuse.

items.title: The tuk-tuk truth
items.description: The tuk-tuk is part of the Bangkok experience but not a means of transport: fix the price before boarding and use it for one short, joyful ride. The '20-baht city tour' offer is not a ride but a shop tour — decline politely.

callout.label: River tip
callout.text: In the late afternoon board an orange-flag boat at Sathorn pier and ride the river into sunset: you pass Wat Arun as its lights come on. The same view from a rooftop bar costs fifty times more — the boat fare is pocket change.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Bangkok choosing a neighborhood means choosing a rhythm: riverside grace, Sukhumvit's night pulse, or the temple mornings of the old city.

local_word.definition: The side street branching off a main road: the key to every Bangkok address. Known by number — Sukhumvit Soi 38 — and each soi is its own world: a night market in one, silent apartments in the next. Getting to know the city begins when you leave the main road and turn into the sois.

items.name: Riverside
items.description: Terraced hotels along the Chao Phraya: river mist at dawn, boat lights at night. Connected to the temples by boat — Bangkok's calmest and most photogenic way to wake up.

items.name: Sukhumvit (Thonglor–Asok)
items.description: Rooftop bars, restaurants and nightlife along the BTS line: the city's modern face. Thonglor is polished, Asok is buzzing — sitting on the train line makes everything easy.

items.name: Old city (Banglamphu)
items.description: Around the Grand Palace and Khao San: walking distance to the temples, plenty of guesthouses and boutique hotels. Far from the rail lines — the river boat is this quarter's metro.

items.name: Chinatown (Yaowarat)
items.description: Boutique hotels amid the neon signs and stalls: at night the street becomes one giant open-air restaurant. The MRT now reaches it — the center of any food-first visit.

items.name: Ari
items.description: A calm neighborhood north on the BTS: third-wave coffee, design cafes and family-run eateries. Off the tourist track — for waking up in the locals' Bangkok.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Bangkok's calendar is measured in rain, not temperature: November–February is the golden window, and April is the water fight of Songkran.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Peak Heat and Songkran
items.subtitle: Spring · The year's hottest, the water festival
items.description: March to May is Bangkok on oven setting: above 35°C with humidity. But mid-April brings Songkran — for Thai New Year the whole city takes to a three-day water fight. It's the most entertaining way ever devised to endure the heat.

callout.label: Songkran tip
callout.text: Staying dry on April 13–15 is impossible: put your phone in a waterproof pouch, don't wear white, join the battle. Silom and Khao San are the main battlefields — leave valuables at the hotel and surrender to sanuk.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Monsoon Green
items.subtitle: Summer · Afternoon downpours, low-season prices
items.description: Monsoon downpours usually fall in the afternoon and pass within the hour: mornings are for touring, the rain break is for a cafe. Hotels get cheaper, temples get quieter — a generous season for those who keep plans flexible.

callout.label: Downpour note
callout.text: When the rain starts, Grab prices surge and traffic locks up: wait it out wherever you are — most showers don't last an hour. Keep a thin raincoat in your bag and a radar app on your phone.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The Rain's Farewell
items.subtitle: Autumn · Last downpours, a swelling river
items.description: September is the wettest month and October closes the curtain: the river runs high, the air is washed clean, and the calm before high season settles in. By late October the city begins to glow for Loy Krathong — the last window of uncrowded Bangkok.

callout.label: October tip
callout.text: Come in late October: the rain has retreated and high-season prices haven't begun. If you catch Loy Krathong on the November full moon, flowered candles are set afloat on the river — Bangkok's most graceful night.

items.label: Winter
items.name: The Golden Season
items.subtitle: Winter · Cool evenings, open skies
items.description: November to February is Bangkok's reward: humidity drops, evenings cool, skies clear. Street tables, rooftop bars and temple mornings are at their most delicious. The world knows it too — hotels fill and prices climb.

callout.label: December tip
callout.text: A December evening is 25°C: reach the rooftop bar half an hour before sunset and watch the city switch its lights on. Mind the dress code — shorts and sandals won't get past the door.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Bangkok is the street-food capital of the world: wok fire, coriander perfume, the balance of hot-sour-sweet-salty — all on a plastic stool.

local_word.definition: Thai for 'delicious': the word you'll hear and say fifty times a day in Bangkok. Give the vendor a thumbs up and say 'aroi!' — a smile is guaranteed; say 'aroi mak mak' (very, very delicious) and the portion may even grow. In this city, praising the food is the most cherished form of thanks.

items.name: Pad thai and the wok stalls
items.description: Rice noodles, shrimp, tamarind sauce and peanuts: ready in a minute over wok fire. Buy from a stall with a local queue, then play with the four seasonings on the table (chili, sugar, fish sauce, vinegar) to find your own balance.
items.tag: Stall classic · with the four seasonings

items.name: Tom yum and the curry table
items.description: Sour-spicy shrimp tom yum, green curry and massaman: an orchestra of lemongrass, galangal and coconut milk. Don't forget to state your spice level — 'pet nit noi' (just a little spicy) is a life-saving sentence.
items.tag: You set the heat · pet nit noi

items.name: The Yaowarat night crawl
items.description: When Chinatown's neon flickers on, the stalls appear: grilled seafood, Chinese-style sweets, fresh fruit. Don't commit to one stall — five stops, five small plates is the correct reading of Yaowarat.

items.name: Boat noodles (kuaytiaw ruea)
items.description: The mini-bowl noodle soup once sold from boats: dark, spiced, gone in a few spoonfuls. Building a tower of bowls at the canal-side stalls near Victory Monument is tradition — five bowls is a warm-up.

items.name: Mango sticky rice
items.description: Ripe mango, coconut-milk sticky rice and crisp mung beans on top: the calling card of Thai desserts. Peak season is April to June, but a good stall finds ripe fruit year-round — the rice should be warm, the mango cold.

items.name: Cha yen and a jok morning
items.description: The orange iced milk tea, cha yen, is the antidote to the heat; in the morning, a bowl of jok (rice porridge with ginger and egg) starts the day gently. Both are the daily poetry of the street stall.

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: In Bangkok the measure of trust is the queue and the turnover: a stall whose ingredients melt away and get replenished before your eyes is always fresh. The air-conditioned 'tourist Thai' restaurant sells the same dish at triple the price and half the flavor — courage is sitting down on the stool.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees the Grand Palace; these six are Bangkok's river-scented, neighborhood-scale hidden face.

items.name: Talad Noi
items.description: Chinatown's back lanes running down to the river: machine-part workshops, street art, centuries-old shrine courtyards and river-view coffee shops. Bangkok's most photogenic place to get lost — close the map and walk.

items.name: Bang Krachao
items.description: The peninsula in the river's bend: a palm-shaded other world five minutes away by long-tail boat. Rent a bicycle and pedal the elevated concrete paths through the jungle — on weekends the Bang Nam Phueng floating market opens too.

items.name: Wang Lang Market
items.description: A local market on the west bank, fed by hospital workers: southern Thai food, dessert makers and cheap tailors. Get off at the pier the tourist boats skip — lunchtime is its liveliest hour.

items.name: Kudeejeen
items.description: The old Portuguese quarter behind Wat Arun: Santa Cruz Church, bakeries making ancestral 'khanom farang' cakes, and riverside footpaths. Three faiths, one neighborhood — a quiet summary of Bangkok's layered past.

items.name: Wat Paknam
items.description: An emerald universe inside a giant green glass stupa: the ceiling fresco opens like outer space, and a 69-meter Buddha towers outside. Reached by MRT — off the tourist track, Bangkok's most otherworldly temple interior.

items.name: The Jim Thompson House
items.description: The teak house complex of the American who introduced Thai silk to the world: tropical garden, antique collection, and the story of its owner vanishing without a trace in the jungle in 1967. A half-hour time journey in the middle of the city.

callout.label: River strategy
callout.text: Bangkok's hidden corners line up along the river: Kudeejeen in the morning, Wang Lang at noon, Talad Noi in the late afternoon, Bang Krachao the next day. Crack the pier-and-boat combination and you cross from tourist Bangkok into the locals' Bangkok.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Bangkok's games have run unchanged for half a century, and all are played with a smile; know the script and pass through smiling.

items.name: The '20-baht city tour' tuk-tuk
items.description: The unbelievably cheap tour ferries you to gem, tailor and souvenir shops: the driver collects commission, you lose hours and sometimes money.
items.instead: Negotiate a real-price short ride, or treat the tuk-tuk as a one-time joy. The moment you hear the 'special day, gasoline coupon' story, smile and walk away.

items.name: The 'temple is closed today' script
items.description: A 'helpful' stranger near the palace gate: 'Closed until noon — let me show you other temples' — the route ends in a shop. The palace is open nearly every day.
items.instead: Check opening hours yourself and walk to the ticket window: trust no 'closed' except from uniformed staff. The same game is played at the river piers.

items.name: Meterless taxis and pier games
items.description: Taxis waiting in tourist zones quote round numbers instead of the meter; some pier touts steer you toward a pricey private boat.
items.instead: 'Meter, please' — if refused, smile, step out, call a Grab. On the river, ask for the orange-flag express boat: a private long-tail only makes sense for a group, with a negotiated price.

items.name: Gem and tailor 'opportunities'
items.description: 'Last day of the government gem sale' or 'a bespoke suit in 24 hours': the stones are glass, the suits are one-fitting wonders.
items.instead: Leave gem-buying out of this trip entirely; if you want a tailor, choose one recommended by your hotel, with at least two fittings and a reasonable deposit. No 'opportunity' that approaches you on the street is one.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Bangkok, the offer that approaches you and the offer you find yourself are different things: to everything that comes to you on the street, say a polite 'mai ao krap/ka' (no thanks). Anger doesn't work in this city — jai yen yen, a cool-hearted smile defuses every game.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From golden temple to neon stall

steps.title: Grand Palace and Wat Pho
steps.description: See the Emerald Buddha at gate opening, then Wat Pho's 46-meter Reclining Buddha: two classics in the morning cool. Shoulders and knees covered.

steps.title: Across the river to Wat Arun
steps.description: Cross from the pier: approach the porcelain-clad spire of the Temple of Dawn. The river breeze is the cure for midday heat.

steps.title: Stall lunch
steps.description: Pad thai or a noodle bowl around Tha Tien: find the local queue, take a plastic stool. Don't forget to say 'aroi!'

steps.title: Jim Thompson House and an AC break
steps.description: A half-hour guided tour of the teak house, then cold air and iced Thai tea in Siam's malls: outsmart the afternoon heat.

steps.title: Sunset boat or rooftop bar
steps.description: Watch the river lights from an orange-flag boat out of Sathorn, or see the city ignite from a rooftop bar — mind the dress code.

steps.title: Yaowarat night
steps.description: A stall crawl under Chinatown's neon: five stops, five plates. Close with mango sticky rice — a Bangkok day ends sweet.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Temples, markets and the green lung — the full Bangkok

steps.title: Classic Bangkok
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: the palace, Wat Pho, Wat Arun, a stall lunch, Jim Thompson, sunset, Yaowarat.

steps.title: Market and neighborhood day
steps.description: If it's a weekend, get lost in Chatuchak market in the morning (go early, grab a section map); afternoon of coffee and wandering in Ari; evening of modern Thai food and soi bars in Thonglor.

steps.title: The far bank
steps.description: Morning boat to Bang Krachao: jungle paths by bicycle and the floating market; Talad Noi street art and river coffee in the late afternoon; farewell dinner of southern Thai food at Wang Lang — the city lights from the boat ride home.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Thai is a tonal language, but these five phrases bring smiles in any tone; end sentences with 'krap' if you're a man, 'ka' if you're a woman.

items.meaning: Hello — paired with the wai (hands together, slight bow), it wins hearts
Thank you — valid currency from stall to temple
Delicious! — the vendor's day brightens, your portion grows
Just a little spicy — life insurance in the Thai kitchen
No problem, never mind — Thailand's 'maalesh'; the answer to every mishap

checklist.title: Bangkok Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Aroi mak mak! You've lived the city of smiles the way it deserves!
